content.title: Response to Reviewer kacd
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful feedback and suggestions. 

## Advantages of the proposed method over SynFlow

We want to emphasize that our method has the following advantages over SynFlow:

1. We prune the model at the **channel level** while SynFlow performs **unstructured sparse** pruning. Therefore, models pruned by our method can immediately enjoy wall-time speedup and memory saving on any commercially-available hardware during both training and inference stages without the need for additional effort. In contrast, the model pruned by SynFlow is unstructured, which results in sparse matrices. 
2. The pruning process of the proposed method is much faster than SynFlow. The process of computing layerwise density in our method can be purely analytical, so the whole pruning process can be done within **one second** for any model on any CPU; while SynFlow requires iteratively forward and backward passes. For example, it takes **15 minutes** to finish the SynFlow pruning process for a ResNet-34 model on ImageNet with an NVIDIA 2080Ti GPU.
3. The proposed method is able to optimize for *both FLOPs count and parameters* while the SynFlow is only able to optimize for parameters. On commodity hardware, CNN models are usually compute-bound, thus FLOPs count is often a more important pruning target. With our formulation, we can optimize for pruning the FLOPs count and/or parameters count in the model, which leads to a more favorable trade-off between accuracy and FLOPs count (as shown in Figure 5(b)).

## Lower baseline accuracy of MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetB0

Due to limited computation resources, we reduce the batch size and training epochs for these two models. We do use the same training recipe for all the MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetB0 models, including baselines, models pruned by SynFlow, and models pruned by our method. 
We agree with the reviewer that the lower baselines would hurt the significance of our claim, thus we refined our training recipe. Because of the time constraint, we focused on EfficientNetB0 only in this rebuttal. We will keep working on refining the training process of MobileNetV2. The new results of EfficientNetB0 are the following and will be updated in the final submission:

| Network        | Methods  | FLOPs(G) | Params(M) | Accuracy (%) |
| -------------- | -------- | -------- | --------- | ------------ |
| EfficientNetB0 | Baseline | 0.40     | 5.29      | 75.7         |
| EfficientNetB0 | SynFlow  | 0.30     | 3.72      | 73.4 (-2.3)  |
| EfficientNetB0 | PreCrop  | 0.30     | 3.67      | 74.2 (-1.5)  |

We tried to use exactly the same training recipe as the original EfficientNet [1] paper but reduced the batch size from 2048 to 1024 due to limited memory. By employing the new training recipe, the accuracy for baseline EffcientNetB0 increases from 73.0% to 75.7%, while the paper reports 76.3%. The overall trend reported in the paper remains the same: The model pruned by PreCrop still has better accuracy compared to the model pruned by SynFlow with the same or fewer parameters and FLOPs


## Comparison with SCP [2]

Our method is significantly different from soft channel pruning (SCP), which optimizes differentiable masks during the training process. 

1. Our method prunes the model before training, which benefits both training and inference. In contrast, SCP keeps the weights and computes the gradient for all channels during training thus it only benefits the inference phase.
2. SCP introduces differentiable masks as more trainable parameters and uses Gumbel-softmax to optimize them. This method further increases the cost of the training process.
3. Our method is data-agnostic, whereas SCP requires training to make the pruning decision. 

References:

    [1] Gale, et al. "Sparse GPUkernels for deep learning", SC’20
    [2] Kang, et al. "Operation-aware soft channel pruning using differentiable masks", ICML’20
    [3] Shen, et al. "When to Prune? A Policy towards Early Structural Pruning", CVPR’22
    [4] Yvinec, et al. "RED: Looking for Redundancies for Data-FreeStructured Compression of Deep Neural Networks", NeurIPS’21
    [5] Rachwan, et al. "Winning the Lottery Ahead of Time: Efficient Early Network Pruning", ICML’22 
    [6] Liu, et al. "Sparse training via boosting pruning plasticity with neuroregeneration", NeurIPS’21
    [7] Liu, et al. "Do we actually need dense over-parameterization? in-time over-parameterization in sparse training", ICML’21

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors proposed SynExp as a proxy for accuracy and format pruning at initialization as an optimization problem to maximize SynExp. Based on this, they proposed PreCrop for channel pruning and PreConfig for channel optimization, both at the initialization. Experimental results show the proposed method can further improve existing models like EfficientNet and MobileNetV2 in terms of accuracy vs. model size trade-off.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Firstly, the paper is generally well-written and easy to follow. 
2. The proposed heuristic to estimate the network's performance outperforms existing ones on the ablation benchmark.
3. Compared to the existing PAI method SynFlow, the proposed method has a better FLOPs/params vs. accuracy trade-off at an even coarser granularity. 

Weakness:
1. Apart from PAI methods, the proposed method uses a very similar setting as zero-shot neural architecture search (NAS) (e.g., [a, b, c]) when only the channel dimension is searched (zero-shot NAS also needs to estimate the performance of a model architecture before training and compare different architectures to pick out a good one). The paper should reference such literature and compare the proposed method with zero-shot NAS, especially the performance estimation function.  We can keep the search space the same (i.e., only the channel dimension) and use the model performance estimator from zero-shot NAS literature for comparison to see if the proposed method is better. 
2. Although the proposed method aims for a training-free setting, it would be better to also include a comparison with post-training pruning results to see how large the gap is.  
3. In the paper, it says, "The SynExp Invariance Theorem shows that the pruning granularity of PAI methods should not affect the accuracy of the pruned model". However, in real cases, the granularity could affect the performance of pruning by a lot (e.g., fine-grained pruning can achieve a larger learning rate). How do we explain the contradiction?

[a] Zhang and Jia, GradSign: Model Performance Inference with Theoretical Insights
[b] Lin et al., Zen-NAS: A Zero-Shot NAS for High-Performance Deep Image Recognition
[c] Mellor et al., Neural architecture search without training
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity, quality, and reproducibility are good. 
In terms of novelty, the proposed method is quite similar to existing PAI and zero-shot NAS methods, with only the difference in the model performance estimator (i.e., SynExp). However, there is no evidence to show SynExp can outperform existing estimators (only compared with SynFlow, which has been outperformed by recent work like [a]).

[a] Zhang and Jia, GradSign: Model Performance Inference with Theoretical Insights
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the proposed method aims to solve an important problem. However, it lacks a comprehensive comparison to existing PAI/zero-shot NAS work, which makes the contribution less convincing. The core novelty also highly depends on whether SynExp is actually better than existing ones.

content.comment:
## Comparison with post-training pruning

We include the comparison on ResNet on ImageNet between the proposed method and two representative post-training channel pruning methods: FPGM [11], and SFP [12]:

| Model    | Method         | Accuracy (baseline / pruned) | FLOPs Reduction (%) |
| -------- | -------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------- |
| ResNet50 | FPGM [11]      | 76.2 / 75.5 (-0.7)           | 42.2                |
| ResNet50 | SFP [12]       | 76.2 / 74.6 (-1.6)           | 41.8                |
| ResNet50 | PreCrop (ours) | 75.0 / 72.4 (-2.6)           | 27.0                |
|          |                |                              |                     |
| ResNet34 | FPGM [11]      | 73.9 / 72.5 (-1.4)           | 41.1                |
| ResNet34 | SFP [12]       | 73.9 / 71.8 (-2.1)           | 41.8                |
| ResNet34 | PreCrop (ours) | 73.5 / 71.5 (-2.0)           | 25.0                |

Although the post-training channel pruning methods achieve better accuracy FLOPs trade-off compared to the proposed methods, post-training pruning methods usually require an expensive fine-tuning process to recover their accuracy loss. For example, in FPGM, the cost of finetuning is set to be the same as the training. Due to the huge difference in cost, we do not compare the proposed method with the post-training pruning approaches in the paper. 
## Counterintuitive claim?

In the paper, we claim the following and provided a rigorous proof. 

> The SynExp Invariance Theorem shows that the pruning granularity of **PAI methods** should not affect the accuracy of the pruned model

It is important to note that our claim only applies to **PAI (pruning-at-initialization) setting**, as we use the fact that all weights are drawn from random distributions. Intuitively, it is because we cannot tell which weights are superior before training. Therefore, structured pruning can be equally good as unstructured pruning. 

For training-based pruning, our claim is not applicable anymore.

content.title: Response to Reviewer seit [1/2]
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion to make necessary comparisons with related work. We have added experiments to compare our approach with zero-shot NAS and post-training pruning methods. 

## Comparison with zero-shot NAS

 We thank the reviewer for pointing out more related work in the field of zero-shot NAS [5, 6, 7]. We will discuss and cite these related works in this paper in the next revision. We do not compare our method with zero-shot NAS methods  because our proposed method differs from zero-shot NAS methods in the following aspects: 

1. The **search space** is different. The typical search space of NAS methods includes width, depth, input resolution, and choice of building blocks.  However, each dimension in the search space is restricted to a few discrete choices to avoid exponential growth of the entire search space [8, 9]. For example, the search space of the channel width usually only contains a limited set of integer values (e.g. channel width $w \in \mathcal{W}=\{24, 32, 40\}$ in [10]). In contrast, our method only focuses on optimizing the width dimension, but we can analytically compute the channel width. Therefore, our search space essentially covers all positive integers (i.e. channel width $w \in \mathbb{N}^+$).
2. The **search budget** is different. Although the cost of zero-shot NAS is significantly reduced from sample-based NAS, it still requires the assistance of expensive RS [1], REINFORCE [2], HyperBand [3], or REA [4] to interact with the huge search space. The computation of GradSign and NASWOT requires forward and backprop of the network. For example, the typical runtime budget for [5] is 12,000 seconds using GPUs, while our method only requires 1 second with a CPU to predict the network. Considering that the typical training time for a ResNet20 model on CIFAR-10 is around an hour, the cost of zero-shot NAS is indeed several orders of magnitude higher than our method. 
3. **Better performance**: We empirically show that our proposed method is able to identify better models in the width dimension through the following two experiments: 
**Popular NAS performance estimators failed to identify the superioress of the PreConfig model.** We use two popular performance estimators used in NAS methods, GradSign[5] and NASWOT[6], to estimate the performance of baseline EfficientNetB0 and EffcientNetB0 after PreConfig. The PreConfig model achieves 0.3% higher accuracy with the same FLOPs and only 81% parameters, thus the PreConfig model is superior to the baseline model. Note that the EfficientNet family is also designed by NAS [10], but PreConfig is able to further improve it. In the following experiment, we report the estimated score of GradSign and NASWOT based on 10 runs. 

| Estimator | Score of EfficientNet | Score of PreConfig EfficientNet |
| --------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| GradSign  | 1.61*10^8             | 1.54*10^8                       |
| NASWOT    | 952.3                 | 952.2                           |
| SynExp    | 9.54*10^30            | 5.68*10^31                      |

From this table, only SynExp gives a higher score for the PreConfig model while the NASOT and GradSign give it a lower score. That means, GradSign and NASWOT cannot identify the PreConfig model as a better model. The results of this experiment empirically demonstrate that popular NAS performance estimators failed to identify the PreConfig model better compared to the baseline model.

Although our method can outperform zero-shot NAS in searching model width, our method does have the limitation that it cannot be used to explore other hyperparameters of the network design.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer seit [1/2]

content.title: Reviewer Feedback
content.comment:
Thanks for the reply. 
1. Indeed, NAS and pruning focus on different search spaces, but the zero-shot NAS algorithms are agnostic to the search space design. So we can actually apply them to a similar search space as pruning.
2. Although zero-shot NAS papers usually do not use a search space with very fine-grained channel options (like every integer), there is no evidence that we need to search such a fine granularity to get good results. Actually, some pruning work just uses a sparse step size like multiples of 8/16/32 to ensure hardware efficiency (better cache alignment). So I don't think it is necessarily a problem. Furthermore, we can always extend NAS to search on a fine-grained channel space since they are agnostic to the search space. 
3. The provided comparison does not guarantee the proposed method is better than NAS. The ranking from NAS is usually noisy: there is a roughly positive relationship between the predicted score and the final score, but not a strict relationship. It is normal for NAS to make a wrong ranking for a specific architecture pair. The question is, when we use the NAS algorithm, is the **best** model we find better than the proposed method or not?

It would be much more convincing if the authors could run the zero-shot NAS algorithm (even on the sparse channel grid, like three options per layer) to get the result for comparison.

content.title: Further response
content.comment:
Thank you for your additional comments. 

We want to clarify that our method is not intended to be superior than zero-shot nas in terms of accuracy. The goal of this method is to provide a super-fast way for pruning channel dimensions. Although the computational cost of the proposed method is significantly less than the zero-shot nas, it can still provide at least comparable performance foring search over the width dimension. 

### More accuracy evaluation
Due to time constraints, we are unable to change the APIs in zero-shot nas codebase to search within our search space. We performed another experiment that has been widely used in the nas literature, that is, evaluating the Spearman correlation $\rho$ between scores and model accuracy. Because all models in the popular NAS benchmark (NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201) have a fixed channel width for the main branch, we handcrafted the following small search space for our experiments. Given a baseline model, we randomly choose a width multiplier $s\in$ { $0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0$ } with equal probability. A new model is then generated by changing the width of the baseline model according to the width multiplier. We obtain the GradSign, NASWOT, SynExp scores, and model accuracy of the generated models. We sampled 50 models from this space for ResNet and VGG16 respectively and reported the Spearman’s correlation $\rho$ between the accuracy and score. We also report the overall runtime for the score evaluation. 
|          | Spearman’s ρ | Time |
| -------- | ------- | ---- | 
| GradSign | 0.540   | 8600s |
| NASWOT   | 0.678   | 1100s |
| SynExp   | 0.682   | 30s |

*GradSign and NASWOT scores are obtained using ten input batches. Evaluation of SynExp score does not require input. 

As shown in the table, our proposed method has slightly better Spearman’s correlation $\rho$ compared to the popular zero-shot nas method with significantly less time. The results indicate that SynExp has a slightly higher rank correlation with accuracy compared to GradSign and NASWOT in this search space.  

### Computational cost comparison
It is important to note that the overall computational budget required for zero-shot nas is significantly greater than that of our method:
Zero-shot nas is an expensive process, even for small search spaces. For example, the above search space has $5^{16}$ models which would be impossible to evaluate exhaustively using zero-shot nas metrics. In order to explore such a search space, other algorithms, such as REINFORCE or REA, must be employed. The time budget, as a hyper-parameter, needs to be set for these algorithms, and the typical time budget for GradSign is 12,000 seconds using GPUs. Given that the typical training time for a Resnet-20 on CIFAR-10 is approximately an hour, zero-shot nas is more costly than training the model itself. As such, it is more appropriate to compare zero-shot nas to training-based channel pruning methods, as they have similar computational costs. 
In contrast, our method is much faster and only requires 1 second with a CPU to solve for the optimal network analytically. It is not fair to compare methods with such disparate computational requirements.

We hope we have addressed all of your concerns, please let us know if there are any additional comments, questions, or concerns.

Later on, the authors propose two techniques, PreCrop and PreConfig, that prune the model structurally and adjust the models' parameters, respectively. PreCrop solves a convex optimization problem that results in an optimal structure, while PreCrop optimizes the models' structures in place. Experiments show the empirical performance of the proposed techniques.

content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Questions:
- Equation (4) says that the expectation on the scores is the same with fixed values of $\{p_l\}$ and is independent of the pruning granularity. The authors then use this fact to claim that the trained CNN is expected to have similar accuracy. Say one score is associated with one trained model accuracy, then how could the mean of the scores be associated with individual models' accuracy? If the variance of the scores is small then it is somewhat arguably, however the authors do not show this point which makes me feel less convinced. 
- Then, the proposed optimization problem in (5), though somewhat empirically effective, is not theoretically justified. Problem (5) is agnostic to the initial weights of neural networks, while SynFlow (and other PAI methods) knows the initial weights, which means they do have additional information on the model training process. The proposed algorithm, however, does not have this information but achieves superior performance without twisting fundamentally the pruning algorithm (i.e., it is still using SynFlow as a scoring function after all). So, it is somehow surprising to me that the proposed algorithm can outperform SynFlow. What is the standard deviation in Table 1? Is it possible that the performance advantage is not statistically significant?
- Following on the previous question, we can come up with an extreme distribution of initial weights to downgrade the performance. For example, the performance is likely to drop if we put $0$ in those un-pruned weights. Solving problem (5) only results in a structure that is agnostic to certain initial weights, 
- It would be better to use a smaller line size in Figure 5 as the two lines are overlapping a lot.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Ss1f [2/2]
content.comment:
## The rationale for using the expectation of the SynFlow score

Next, we prove that *at a given sparsity level*, when the score has a large variance while the accuracy has a small variance, using the expectation of the score leads to a proxy for accuracy with less error compared to using the score as a proxy for accuracy.
**Theorem 2**: For any function $f$ that maps SynFlow score $\mathcal{S}$ to test the accuracy of the model $y$, we use $\hat f$ as an estimator of $f$, and $h$ as a function represents random perturbation. If random perturbation $h$ does not change the expectation of the accuracy, we have $\mathbb{E}_h[f(h(\mathcal{S}))] = f(\mathcal{S})$. Then we can prove that $\mathbb{E}_h[\hat f (h(\mathcal{S})]$ is a better estimation of $f(\mathcal{S})$ compared to $\hat f(S)$ in terms of $L_2$ norm error.
**Proof**: 
$$
\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{S}[\|\mathbb{E}_h[\hat f (h(\mathcal{S}))] - f(\mathcal{S})\|^2] = \
\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{S}[\|\mathbb{E}_h[\hat f (h(\mathcal{S})) - f(h(\mathcal{S}))]\|^2] \le \
\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{S}[\mathbb{E}_h[\|\hat f (h(\mathcal{S})) - f(h(\mathcal{S}))\|^2]] = \
\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{S}[\|\hat f (\mathcal{S}) - f(\mathcal{S})\|^2] 
$$

Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is used in the second step as $\|\cdot\|^2$ is convex. $\square$


Hope the additional theoretical proof and empirical evidence can resolve the reviewer's concern about using the expectation of SynFlow as the proxy.

## Why would the expectation of SynFlow outperform SynFlow score with less information?
> Problem (5) is agnostic to the initial weights of neural networks, while SynFlow (and other PAI methods) knows the initial weights, which means they do have additional information on the model training process.

It is because, in this PAI setting, the weight position and value are not helpful to predict accuracy. This additional information is essentially **biased** since when using the weight position and value to compute the SynFlow score, *at a given sparsity level,* the SynFlow score is not linearly correlated to the model accuracy. That is to say, this part of additional information is not useful to predict a better model architecture. 

## How does extreme distribution affect the performance of PreCrop
> For example, the performance is likely to drop if we put 0 in those un-pruned weights.

There are two reasons we cannot do so:

1. In the proof of Theorem 1 in the appendix, we assume that the distribution of weights is the same for all different granularities to achieve our conclusion. If we put 0 in the unpruned weights for any pruned pattern, that essentially changes the distribution of the weights. In that case, we cannot come to the same conclusion. 
2. In the paper, we assume that the model after PreCrop is densely parameterized. If zeros are put in the unpruned weights, that changes the dense weight to sparse. It also breaks our assumption. 
## Width of the figure

The previous width of the figure is indeed too wide. We will update the figures in the final submission.

References:

    [1] Su, et al. "Sanity-checking pruning methods: Random tickets can win the jackpot", NeurIPS’21
    [2] Frankle, et al. "Pruning neural networks at initialization: Why are we missing the mark?", ICLR’20

content.title: Response to Reviewer Ss1f [1/2]
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the critical feedback on our main theorem. We added additional theoretical and empirical support below to address the key issues raised by the reviewer. We will update Section 3.2 accordingly.

We use the expectation of SynFlow (SynExp) as the proxy for model accuracy in our paper, and we will justify why this is a better choice compared to using the SynFlow score in the following sections. 

In the following sections, we first evaluated the SynFlow scores and accuracy of the model pruned by SynFlow as well as other models obtained by randomly shuffling and/or re-initializing the weights of the pruned model. We empirically found that the variance of the accuracy of the models is small, while the variance of the SynFlow scores is large.
.Then we prove that, under this condition, the expectation of the SynFlow Score is **an accuracy proxy with less error** compared to using the SynFlow score. 
## The variance of the model accuracy is small



We further empirically demonstrate the small variance in the accuracy of models if randomly shuffled and reinitialized. Figures 1, 3, and 5 in the paper depict all experiments on CIFAR-10, with error bars obtained from 3-5 runs of the same experiment. We can clearly see from the figures that there is a small variance in the accuracy of the models pruned by SynFlow.  We further performed the following experiment for rebuttal: after pruning with SynFlow score, we first randomly shuffle the weight mask and randomly initialize the weight, then we evaluate the test accuracy and the SynFlow score of the new model. We repeat the experiment for 10 runs at 4 different sparsities with ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10. We also compute the Spearman correlation coefficient **ρ** ($\rho$) between SynFlow score and accuracy for each run and coefficient of variation **CV** ($c_v = \frac{\sigma}{\mu}$) for accuracy and SynFlow score:
| Sparsity | Acc (mean/std) | CV of Acc | SynFlow (mean/std) | CV of SynFlow | ρ     |
| -------- | -------------- | --------- | ------------------ | ------------- | ----- |
| 0.03     | 76.02 / 0.58   | 7.6*10^-3 | 2.67 / 0.36        | 1.3*10^-1     | 0.16  |
| 0.14     | 85.39 / 0.48   | 5.6*10^-3 | 3.09 / 0.42        | 1.4*10^-1     | -0.19 |
| 0.30     | 88.05 / 0.36   | 4.1*10^-3 | 3.48 / 0.45        | 1.3*10^-1     | -0.08 |
| 0.46     | 88.85 / 0.39   | 4.4*10^-3 | 3.50 / 0.52        | 1.5*10^-1     | -0.54 |

## The variance of the SynFlow score is large
The following two conclusions can be drawn from the CIFAR-10 experiment:

1. After randomly shuffling the weight and randomly reinitializing the weight, because the coefficient of variation (CV) of accuracy is much smaller than that of the SynFlow score, we validate that the variance of accuracy is small and the variance of the SynFlow is large.
2. Remember that Spearman correlation coefficient $\rho \in [-1, 1]$, and it reveals the rank correlation between two random variables. Here, the Spearman correlation coefficient $\rho$ between SynFlow score and accuracy is close to $0$, and sometimes it is even negative. It indicates that *at the same sparsity*, given the higher SynFlow score, we cannot predict model accuracy will be higher or lower; when the Spearman correlation coefficient $\rho$ is negative, a higher SynFlow score is more likely to result in lower model accuracy.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studied the problem of structured Pruning-at-initialization (PAI) on CNNs. It first introduced synaptic expectation (SynExp) as a proxy metric for accuracy. Then, this paper formulated an optimization problem to maximize SynExp for determining the layer-wise pruning ratios, which are subject to model size/FLOPs constraints. The authors observed empirically and prove theoretically that the accuracy of CNN models pruned by PAI depends on the layer-wise density. Experiments are conducted on several CNN architectures like ResNet, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet, on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets to verify their statement and proposed method.

content.title: Response to Reviewer CtCn
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed assessment of our work. Below are our responses to address the key concerns.

## More baselines other than SynFlow

To the best of our knowledge, there is no follow-up work using the same setting as SynFlow to prune CNNs before training. 
We exhaustively examined all the publications that cited SynFlow and other related papers in the area of pruning-at-initialization (PAI). We have not found any follow-up work that use the same setting as SynFlow. Please see below for a more detailed summary of our literature search. 
Since recent efforts in [8, 9, 10] revealed several deficiencies in existing PAI methods, no major progress has been made in this direction without addressing these deficiencies. In fact, this is the very focus of our paper.

According to our literature search, the related papers that cite SynFlow fall into the following three categories:

1. The deficiencies of SynFlow (detailed discussed in our paper). [9, 10, 11]
2. Appling the SynFlow score metric to other tasks, such as zero-cost NAS and Transformer pruning. e.g. [4, 6, 8]
3. Other pruning methods that are inspired by SynFlow, but prune at stages other than at-initialization: such as a) pruning after pre-training [3], b) pruning during training [7], and c) pruning early in training [2, 5]. Though pruning at later stages might increase the model's accuracy, PAI methods provide the most speedup and memory saving during the training process. The trade-off between pruning-at-initialization and pruning at later stages is out of the scope of this paper.

## Similar layer-wise density compared to SynFlow

Yes, we do have a similar layer-wise density in Figure 2 and Table 1. It is because our SynExp metric (SynFlow Expectation) is based on the SynFlow score. We emphasize that our method has the following advantages over SynFlow:

1. We prune the model at the **channel level** while SynFlow performs **unstructured sparse** pruning. Therefore, models pruned by our method can immediately enjoy wall-time speedup and memory saving on any commercially-available hardware during both training and inference stages without the need for additional effort. In contrast, the model pruned by SynFlow is unstructured, which results in sparse matrices. 
2. The pruning process of the proposed method is much faster than SynFlow. The process of computing layerwise density in our method can be purely analytical, so the whole pruning process can be done within **one second** *for any model on any CPU; while SynFlow requires iteratively forward and backward passes. For example, *it takes* **15 minutes** to finish the SynFlow pruning process for a ResNet-34 model on ImageNet with an NVIDIA 2080Ti GPU.
3. The proposed method is able to optimize for *both FLOPs count and parameters* while the SynFlow is only able to optimize for parameters. On commodity hardware, CNN models are usually compute-bound, thus FLOPs count is often a more important pruning target. With our formulation, we can optimize for pruning the FLOPs count and/or parameters count in the model, which leads to a more favorable trade-off between accuracy and FLOPs count (as shown in Figure 5(b)).

## Results on ResNet-50
We have added experiments on ResNet-50 following the same setup as the other experiments in Table 1. The results are summarized in the table below, where an asterisk (*) indicates that the numbers do not take into account the overhead of sparse matrices in storage and computation.

| Network  | Methods  | FLOPs(G) | Params(M) | Accuracy (%) |
| -------- | -------- | -------- | --------- | ------------ |
| ResNet50 | Baseline | 3.85     | 25.56     | 75.0         |
| ResNet50 | SynFlow  | 2.82*    | 12.81*    | 73.3 (-1.7)  |
| ResNet50 | PreCrop  | 2.81     | 12.74     | 72.4 (-2.6)  |
The results on ResNet-50 also support our claim thatPreCrop can achieve similar accuracy as SynFlow with comparable FLOPs and parameter counts while etaining the structured dense model.

content.title: Common response
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive reviews. We appreciate the positive comments on our work(e.g., "the method is interesting", "conceptually simple yet seem to be effective", and good empirical results on multiple dataset and model architectures) and have addressed the main concerns raised by the reviewers in our responses  

## Main concerns
We summarize the key concerns raised by the reviewers and how we addressed them in the rebuttal process as follows:

1. Lack of comparison with other model compression methods.
Other compression methods include other related works of SynFlow (Reviewer CtCn), zero-shot nas (Reviewer seit), and other soft channel pruning methods (Reviewer kacd). In our rebuttal, we emphasize that there is a **significant distinction** between our approach and the methods mentioned by the reviewers, especially in terms of the computational cost. Our method only requires less than **1 second** of CPU time and will benefit both **training** and inference phases on commodity hardware, while other methods have significantly larger computation overhead. 


2. Using the expectation of SynFlow is not well-supported.
This problem mainly comes from Reviewer Ss1f. With additional theoretical and empirical support, we justify why using the expectation of SynFlow is a better choice than using the SynFlow score as the proxy for model accuracy.

3. More empirical results.
We added more empirical results for ResNet50 requested by Reviewer CtCn, a comparison with post-training pruning requested by Reviewer seit, and better baseline results requested by Reviewer kacd.

We hope that our response answers the reviewers' questions. If anything still remains unclear to the reviewers or AC, we are glad to provide further clarification.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
**Summary:** This paper proposes a method for pruning neural networks at initialization at the channel granularity. 

**Strengths:**
* The paper makes an interesting observation: for the accuracy of existing PAI methods, it is possible to prune at a larger granularity (specifically the channel granularity) without further hurting accuracy. The paper shows this theoretically and empirically. The downside is that this is within a range of the relatively poor accuracy that existing PAI methods get, but it's a nice improvement to at least get that performance in a way that is easy to accelerate.

**Weaknesses:** I work in the pruning-at-initialization space, and I echo several of the reviewer's comments on this paper:
* "SynExp is invariant to weight shuffling and reinitialization" - This statement reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the literature on PAI. This is implied to be a benefit of the method, but it is instead a flaw. Su et al. and Frankle et al. both show that this is an indication of the poor performance of existing methods like SNIP, GraSP, and SynFlow and the potential inherent difficulty of pruning at initialization. It is desirable to be sensitive to weight shuffling and reinitialization, since that means the method is choosing specific connections and weights that are important. Specific to channel pruning (the focus of this paper), Li et al. ("Rethinking the Value of Network Pruning") show that a variety of then-SOTA structured pruning methods are also invariant to initialization even when pruning after training, so it may be difficult or impossible to do this for any channel pruning, even after initialization.
* One of the reviewers observes that MobileNet and EfficientNet have strangely low baseline accuracies. This is known to affect the ordering of pruning methods (Blalock et al., "What is the state of neural network pruning?"), and this needs to be rectified for the evaluation to carry weight.
* This paper fails to grapple with one of the main challenges with current PAI methods: none of them preserve accuracy at very high sparsities; they all entail an inherent tradeoff between sparsity/FLOPs and accuracy. (This is in contrast to methods for pruning after training, which typically retain accuracy at high sparsities, meaning they are drop-in replacements for existing networks.) The challenge with this tradeoff is that there is no clear way of knowing what a _good_ tradeoff is. Given that this paper does structured pruning, there is actually a good baseline to try: narrower and shallower versions of the same networks (e.g., ResNet-14 or narrower versions of ResNet-20). These are smaller dense networks that may or may not do better than those networks produced by SynExp. If SynExp were to find better dense networks than those produced by simply training a smaller network, that would be a nice win. As it stands, though, there is no way to evaluate whether the tradeoffs found by this paper are worthwhile other than that they are better than a flawed alternative method on a FLOP-basis (on an accuracy basis, the lines are too thick and the y-axis ranges too wide to tell).

**Overall:** I argue in favor of rejection due to the weaknesses noted by the reviewers and others noted above that are common in the PAI literature. At the end of the day, existing PAI methods are quite poor (in terms of performance and in terms of how little aspects like reinitialization, shuffling, and - now - granularity matter). Progress in PAI should address those weaknesses rather than embrace them. The main advance of this paper is to show that PAI results are invariant to the granularity of pruning, which itself is another concerning aspect of the state of affairs when it comes to pruning at initialization.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The current literature on pruning-at-initialization is flawed, and this paper reflects many of those flaws.
